title: Depression and costs of health care
contribution: In claims from 618,780 privately insured patients (D2 Hawkeye), depressed patients had higher median non-mental-health costs in all 11 chronic diseases studied ($1,570 to $15,240 per year; ratios 1.5 to 2.9), the gap persisted across comorbidity-severity levels, and depression and each disease were more prevalent together than apart.
problem_entry: {AP (health care); no optimization model} The interaction of depression with chronic disease 'remains incompletely understood'; prior studies measured cost differences overall or in one disease at a time, never across the most prevalent chronic diseases of one primary-care population, and the cause of the higher cost is unknown (abstract and pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Cross-sectional case-control design on one administrative claims dataset: 'depressed' = depression ICD-9 code AND antidepressant fill, single-criterion patients set aside; per disease, median non-mental-health cost compared in dollars and ratios, by service type, across adapted Charlson index levels, and with cross-prevalences (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Claims for 618,780 self-insured patients enrolled 1 Sep 2004 - 31 Aug 2005, no Medicare/Medicaid (p. 2); 41 ICD-9 codes grouped into 11 diseases requiring 2 outpatient visits or 1 admission (p. 2); study cohort 548,062 (p. 3); admitted limits: low coding sensitivity makes prevalences unusable as absolute measures (p. 5), likely bias toward more severe patients (p. 7), only 14.1% of antidepressant users coded as depressed (p. 8).
proof_devices: n/a as formulation; medians for right-skewed costs with a sensitivity check on means and quartiles, R 2.3.1 (p. 3)
two-channel cohort definition (diagnosis code AND prescription) with the single-channel groups set aside and re-analysed as a check (pp. 3, 8)
severity stratification by an adapted Charlson Comorbidity Index (pp. 3-4, 6)
bias-direction argument: coding-sensitivity bias cancels in ratios, severity bias inflates, undiagnosed controls deflate the difference (pp. 5, 7-8)
significance claims without a named test in the Statistics section (p. 3)
experiments: Higher median non-mental-health cost for depressed patients in all 11 diseases (obesity not significant), $1,570-$15,240, ratios 1.5-2.9 (p. 3); pharmacy the largest component, inpatient only for CAD, epilepsy, CHF (p. 4); mean CCI 0.22 vs 0.15, gap independent of severity per Figure 3 (no text layer) (p. 4); cross-prevalence ratios 1.4-6.8 (p. 4); depressed share given as 3.0% (p. 3) and 2.3% (p. 7).
positioning: Builds on five overall-cost studies and disease-specific studies (diabetes ratios 1.6-4.5, CHF 1.29) and on claims-data methodology (combining diagnosis and prescription codes); novelty claimed as consistency across 11 diseases (pp. 1-2, 4).
writing: Clinical IMRaD paper; most of the discussion goes to artifacts and bias directions, hedged with 'probably' and 'likely'; ends with the stockholding disclosure (pp. 4-8).
limits_future: No causation; no indication whether treating depression would reduce non-mental-health costs (pp. 6, 8); administrative data cannot give absolute prevalence (p. 8); the set-aside single-criterion groups 'merit further study' (p. 8).

method_links.note: Partner (company) data and an honest statement of what the analysis cannot show (step 6), but no owner decision, no current rule as baseline and no decision metric: a descriptive association study.
Company-held claims database (D2 Hawkeye) as data channel; clinical work in a clinical journal (Workflow E step 2); the stockholding is disclosed, as Research Integrity Rule 5 asks.

transferable: Define the exposed cohort by two independent data channels (diagnosis code AND prescription), set aside single-channel groups, and rerun the analysis on them as a check (pp. 3, 8).
With a source of known low sensitivity, report ratios between cohorts and state for each bias whether it cancels in the ratio and, if not, which way it pushes the result (pp. 5, 7-8).
For right-skewed costs, headline medians and rerun with means and quartiles (p. 3).
coauthors: Charles A. Welch (Massachusetts General Hospital; correspondence), David Czerwinski, Bijay Ghimire (joint affiliations MGH, MIT ORC, D2 Hawkeye)

quotes.text: Although these prevalences are not useful as absolute measures, they are useful in comparing the prevalence of chronic comorbid conditions in depressed and non-depressed patients, because the bias applies equally to both the depressed and non-depressed cohorts.
This study does not establish causation in the association between depression and increased non-mental health costs, but several possibilities should be considered.

title: Finite adaptability in multistage linear optimization
contribution: Introduces k-adaptability (k contingency plans, i.e. a k-partition of the uncertainty set) as a hierarchy between static robust and fully adaptable two-stage LPs that accommodates discrete recourse. Proves a geometric explanation of the static-robust gap, dual-based necessary conditions for improvement, a bilinear exact formulation, NP-hardness and tractability for fixed dimension, and gives hyperplane-split heuristics that close 40-70% of the gap on random instances.
problem_entry: {RO; IO (discrete recourse); LO; AP (air traffic) as testbed} Multistage robust problems 'present significant tractability challenges'; static robust is conservative, complete adaptability 'overly optimistic' (unobservable, intractable, costly to implement); no adaptability proposal offers a variable degree of adaptability or handles integer second-stage variables under set-based uncertainty (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Choose k second-stage plans, equivalently partition the uncertainty set into k regions; increasing k bridges static robust (k = 1) and complete adaptability; discrete plans make discrete variables natural; incomparable with affine adaptability (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Two-stage LP, polytopic uncertainty in the matrices, affine in the parameter; static robust assumed feasible (pp. 2-3); a 'relatively mild' Continuity Assumption for convergence, shown necessary (pp. 4-5, 12); random scheduling instances (convex hulls of random or one-row-degraded rate matrices) and a stylized 100-flight storm example (pp. 13-15).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: static robust = complete adaptability over the smallest 'hypercube' containing the set; sandwich with a non-implementable 'utopic' formulation plus duality (p. 4)
Proposition 1: convergence as partitions refine, via compactness and a finite subcover (p. 5)
Propositions 2-3 and Lemma 2: points of a polytope tied to the dual of the static problem map to necessary conditions for epsilon-improvement, sufficient in the single-stage case (pp. 5-7)
Proposition 4: optimal 2-adaptability as a finite bilinear program, by strong duality (pp. 7-8)
Proposition 5: NP-hardness by reduction from Partition, even with RHS uncertainty (pp. 8-9)
Proposition 6: polynomial when min(uncertainty dimension, problem dimension, uncertain constraints) is fixed (pp. 9-10)
Algorithms 1-2: hyperplane splits with normals from extreme-point pairs or facets, quasi-convex search, applied iteratively (pp. 12-13)
extended example: necessary conditions computed with CDD certify that 2 regions cannot help and at least 5 are needed for a given epsilon; affine adaptability equals static robust there (pp. 10-12)
experiments: 6x6 instance: 2- and 4-adaptability close 25.8% and just over 40% of the gap; with binary stations one split reaches the fully adaptable cost (p. 13); 50 instances per category: 4-adaptability closes over 70% for 6x6, dropping to about 52% (and 2-adaptability from over 63% to just over 42%) when the uncertainty set doubles; gap upper-bounded by 500 sampled points so benefits are lower bounds (p. 14); air-traffic Tables III-IV not in the text layer; no solver or run times reported.
positioning: Between static robust and complete adaptability; complementary to the affine adaptability of Ben-Tal et al. (each wins on some example); distinct from stochastic integer recourse and from other NP-hard adaptability proposals (pp. 1-3, 11-12).
writing: Five numbered goals each justified 'point by point'; geometric intuition (Fig. 1) before algebra; an extended example built to illustrate six points of the theory; hedged close: numerical evidence 'indicates that its behavior is good' (pp. 2, 10-12, 16).
limits_future: Optimal partitions are NP-hard and the heuristic carries no guarantee (pp. 7, 16); Proposition 6 tractability is only theoretical (p. 10); full air-traffic model deferred to a technical report and the thesis (pp. 13, 15); future: nonconvex uncertainty sets (elsewhere) and nonconvex constraints (pp. 15-16).

method_links.note: Dual read for structure (Lemma 2, Prop. 2), exact finite reformulation (Prop. 4), boundary printed (Props. 5-6, with 'more than theoretical tractability' needed); heuristics only call a static robust solver, so they inherit its class including discrete variables.

k is a one-integer knob with reported gap closure for k = 2, 4 and printed bad cases (no gain from 2-adaptability in Sec. VI; benefit shrinks as the set grows), but the cost of plans is named without a price and the guarantees are convergence and necessary conditions, not a solution-independent probability bound.

Certificate logic without MIO: necessary conditions certify that k regions cannot achieve epsilon-improvement, and the intractable benchmark is estimated on the side that understates the method; the incumbent class (affine policies) is dueled only on constructed examples.
Thesis-to-journal paper of the RO lineage (Caramanis, MIT PhD 2006), with full models kept in the thesis and a technical report; partition idea later continued in S087 (card s10).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy hierarchy bridging static and fully adaptive
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: One integer k indexes a hierarchy from static robust to complete adaptability; convergence holds under a stated continuity assumption, and a counterexample shows the assumption is needed.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: geometry of the uncertainty set explains the value of adaptivity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lemma 1 locates the static-adaptive gap exactly in the hypercube hull of the uncertainty set (compare S217's symmetry bound).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: conservative-side benchmark bound for an intractable optimum
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Complete adaptability is approximated by 500 sampled points so that the reported share of the gap closed is a lower bound on the true benefit (compare S153's interdiction upper bound).

transferable: Bracket the adaptive problem between the static robust problem and a non-implementable 'utopic' relaxation in which every variable sees the uncertainty, then use duality to locate the gap (p. 4).
Map extreme points of the dual's optimal face to necessary conditions; a few can certify that k plans cannot improve by epsilon (pp. 5-7, 11).
When the ideal benchmark is intractable, estimate it from the side that makes your method look worse and say so with the results (p. 14).
To claim complementarity with an incumbent policy class, construct one example where each class beats the other (pp. 3, 11-12).
coauthors: Constantine Caramanis (UT Austin ECE; his 2006 MIT PhD thesis is ref. [11])

quotes.text: in large scale applications we require more than theoretical tractability
Indeed, all that is required for the algorithms is a method to solve the static robust problem.

title: A discrete optimization approach to supervised ranking
contribution: Workshop version of the Chang-Bertsimas-Rudin MIP for supervised ranking: exact maximization of AUC and of a general class of rank statistics with pairwise binaries and an epsilon margin, reported statistically best on six data sets but with uncertified MIPs and no RRF results (S561 calls it its shorter nonarchival version).
problem_entry: {ML; IO as engine} Ranking methods replace the rank statistic by a convex surrogate; small ranking gains matter (manholes, drug screening, Netflix); optimize the true objective exactly and use it as a benchmark (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Linear scores; binary z_ik per positive-negative pair set to 1 only with margin epsilon (P_AUC); a rank risk functional unifying WRS, partial WMW, WTA, MRR, DCG and P-Norm Push (P_RRF); ties counted as misranks to exclude w = 0; LP relaxation as fast approximation (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Binary labels; w in [-1, 1]^d; epsilon trades speed against generalization (p. 4); six data sets with n_train <= 1,000 and d <= 10, one of them artificial (ROC Flexibility) (pp. 5-6).
proof_devices: MIP formulations P_AUC(epsilon) and P_RRF(epsilon) with pairwise and rank-threshold binaries (pp. 4-5)
strict inequalities so ties count as misranks, excluding the trivial w = 0 (p. 4)
LP relaxation as approximate method (p. 5)
no theorem (n/a)
experiments: Ten random splits vs RankBoost, logistic regression, SVM-style ranking and the LP relaxation; MIP reported statistically highest (matched-pairs t-test, 0.05) everywhere, big gain only on the artificial set (test AUC 81.8 vs 65.9-67.8), LP above MIP by raw mean on two test sets; time limit up to ten hours, not all MIPs optimal, solver unnamed, RRF untested (pp. 5-6).
positioning: Against convex-surrogate ranking (RankBoost, SVM-style, logistic regression); builds on Clemencon-Vayatis rank statistics and on Bertsimas-Shioda CRIO (pp. 1-3).
writing: Six-page workshop paper; applications-first opening; 'benchmark' framing; results hedged as 'Preliminary evidence' (pp. 1-2, 6).
limits_future: Uncertified MIPs within up to ten hours; RRF formulation not yet tested; comprehensive experiments with Gurobi announced (p. 6).

method_links.note: A statistic owned by IR and statistics written exactly as a MIP; one formulation for a whole class of rank statistics (RRF). Count together with S561 (same experiment).
Pre-figure 'why now': the early-1970s intractability belief (via Bertsimas-Shioda) and 'major advances within the last decade', with no number.
Surrogate step replaced by an exact model and incumbents dueled out of sample, but no warm start, no gap and an uncertified 'benchmark' (Tension T1 in 2010).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: promote the evaluation metric to the training objective
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The MIP optimizes the same rank statistic used to evaluate ranking quality, while other methods optimize heuristic surrogate losses (as S470 in s01).

transferable: Count ties against yourself (a tie is a misrank) so that degenerate solutions such as w = 0 cannot score well (p. 4).
Report the LP relaxation of your MIP as a separate competitor to show how much integrality buys (pp. 5-6).
coauthors: Allison Chang (MIT ORC; contact author), Cynthia Rudin (MIT ORC per p. 1)

quotes.text: This means that the cost function that we optimize with MIP is also the measure that we use to evaluate ranking quality, while other methods use heuristic loss functions that differ from the evaluation measure.

Not all of the MIPs solved to provable optimality within the specified time limit – up to ten hours for the larger datasets – so given more time, it is possible that the MIP solutions could be even better.

title: Integer optimization methods for supervised ranking
contribution: MIO formulations that exactly maximize AUC and a unified class of rank statistics (rank risk functionals, including a new staircase statistic), with a theorem that the leaner minimum-rank model is exact when examples are distinct; large gains on an artificial data set, parity on real ones, and most MIOs uncertified at 1-10 h cutoffs.
problem_entry: {ML; IO as engine} Surrogate-loss ranking accommodates huge problems 'at the expense of exact solutions'; 'not all ranking problems are large', and in re-ranking, maintenance or drug discovery 'a better solution is worth the extra computation time'; integer optimization for ranking unexplored (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Two contributions: unify rank statistics in one MIO class from which new statistics follow (staircase statistic for tiered inspection), and a 'guarantee of optimality' or at least a solver bound (pp. 4, 6-7); pessimistic tie-breaking (p. 7); P_AUC, P_RRF,rank, leaner P_RRF,minrank, big-M/SOS variants and pairwise-preference generalization (pp. 13-17).
assumptions: Linear scores with w in [-1, 1]^d; nonlinearity via added features (pp. 5, 13); exactness needs the smallest positive score gap >= epsilon, checked after solving by recomputing AUC (p. 13); data: ROC Flexibility (500 examples, 20 unique), five UCI/LIBSVM sets, Haberman and Pima for DCG@N (pp. 22-27).
proof_devices: formulation-strength argument (relaxation close to the convex hull) citing the IO book; valid inequalities (22)-(25) (pp. 10, 15)
pathological duplicate-data example showing minimum ranks can mislead (p. 18)
Lemma 4 and Theorem 5 relating rank and minimum-rank objectives (p. 19)
Lemma 6: random perturbation w + delta*u breaks ties with probability one while preserving orderings (pp. 20-21)
Theorem 7: with distinct examples a minimum-rank maximizer is a rank maximizer (p. 21)
borrowed speed-up tables: supercomputer gigaflops, PILOTS LP over machines (factor > 6,000), PDS-30 over CPLEX versions (factor 350 in 11 years), shown separately and not multiplied (pp. 10-12)
experiments: RankBoost, LR, SVM-style, P-Norm Push (p = 2, 4, 8) in MATLAB, untuned and unregularized; MIO on Gurobi 3.0.0 (CPLEX 11.2.1 for ROC Flexibility), 2x Xeon E5440, 32 GB; ten splits; ROC Flexibility +11.8% train and +20.6% test relative AUC; real sets within 0.1 test-AUC points, LP above MIO on two; DCG@N wins on ROC Flexibility and Haberman, worst on Pima test; 1-10 h cutoffs, most MIOs not optimal, no gaps (pp. 23-29).
positioning: Against surrogate-loss learning-to-rank (RankBoost, SVM rank, RankNet, P-Norm Push, logistic regression) and ML-meets-discrete-optimization work that uses heuristics; Le-Smola noted as an alternative unification; claims first MIO for ranking (pp. 3, 6-9).
writing: Two named contributions; a tutorial MIO section with a sports-team example and borrowed speed-up tables; abstract claims 'significant advantages' while Sec. 5.3 concedes most runs are uncertified (pp. 2, 4, 9-12, 29).
limits_future: P_RRF,rank too hard except small or sparse problems (p. 22); huge run-time variance; Pima overfits (pp. 27, 29); future: data conditions making the LP relaxation tight, and epsilon and bounds on w as MIO-native regularization (p. 30).

method_links.note: IR/statistics objective written exactly as MIO and unified; new statistic derived from the class; theorem showing when the cheaper formulation is exact; boundary printed for the rank formulation.

2011 'why now': 1970s belief conceded, hardware and software progress shown as separate borrowed LP benchmarks (PILOTS, PDS-30), neither rebuilt nor multiplied; anticipates the LP-for-MIO slippage of the [05 Sec. 1.6] correction.

Exact joint model duels incumbents out of sample, says where it wins (flexible data) and prints a loss (Pima), but the 'guarantee of optimality' meets 'Most of the MIOs did not solve to optimality', no gaps despite the solver-bound argument, no warm starts: Tension T1 six years before OCT.
Student-carried line (workshop, working paper, student-paper competition finalist) continuing the CRIO programme (Bertsimas-Shioda 2007) before the 2014 lens.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: promote the evaluation metric to the training objective
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The objective optimized by MIO is the rank statistic used for evaluation, instead of exponential, hinge or logistic surrogates.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: cheap formulation certified equivalent under a genericity condition
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 7 proves the leaner minimum-rank model exact for distinct examples (via a probability-one perturbation), a duplicate-data counterexample shows the condition matters, and the Pima results confirm equality.

transferable: After solving a margin-based MIO, recompute the true metric from the returned weights to verify the formulation was exact for that epsilon (p. 13).
When a lean formulation can fail on degenerate data, prove a genericity condition under which it is exact and show both a counterexample (p. 18) and an empirical check (p. 27).
Plot solution paths (objective vs time per trial) to show where an MIO stalls and how much run times vary (pp. 29-30).
coauthors: Allison Chang (MIT ORC), Cynthia Rudin (MIT Sloan)

quotes.text: Even if an MIO problem is too large to solve to provable optimality, solvers provide a bound on the optimal objective value, which may be a useful measure of closeness to optimality.
Most of the MIOs did not solve to optimality before the cutoff time indicated in Table 12, in which case the time recorded was the time until the last (possibly suboptimal) solution was found.

title: Ordered rules for classification: A discrete optimization approach to associative classification
contribution: ORC (read in the 2011 ORC working-paper version, 'S448 WP'): one MIO mines the support-coverage frontier of association rules, which contains the optimum of every monotone interestingness measure, and a second MIO orders the rules into a decision list maximizing regularized training accuracy; accuracy on par with SVM, RF and boosting on 11 data sets, with uncertified solves.
problem_entry: {ML; IO as engine} Accurate models (SVM) are not interpretable and interpretable ones (trees) are not 'specifically optimized to achieve the highest accuracy'; associative classifiers order rules by an arbitrary interestingness measure; rule mining meets 'combinatorial explosion' (L! orders); no mathematical-programming approach to decision lists known (WP pp. 2-5).
key_idea: RuleGen MIO traces the support-coverage frontier with no-good ('infeasibility') cuts, extending the Bayardo-Agrawal border to general rules; MIO (15) ranks the rules to maximize training accuracy with a reward on the default rule's rank to shorten the list; interpretability made operational as 'convincing' and 'concise' (WP pp. 2-16).
assumptions: Binary items from binned features, rows with missing values dropped (WP pp. 26-27); eleven data sets (n = 267-2,201, d = 8-41) plus Wine (n = 4,898, d = 44) (WP pp. 18, 24); one parameter setting for all data, chosen in preliminary experiments (WP p. 17); Haberman's year-of-operation feature removed as not predictive (WP p. 26).
proof_devices: rule polytope with 2d binaries and 3n continuous auxiliaries shown to be forced integral (WP pp. 6-7)
partial order on coverage, prevalence and support: the non-dominated frontier contains the optimizers of monotone interestingness measures (Table 4 p. 9; WP pp. 7-9)
no-good 'infeasibility constraints' (12) and (14) to enumerate all optima at a frontier point (WP pp. 10-11)
ranking MIO (15)-(31) with assignment-based ranks, valid inequalities (19)-(20) to improve the relaxation (WP p. 15) and (31) to speed up computation (WP p. 16)
no generalization theorem (n/a)
experiments: Three-fold CV on 11 data sets vs LR, SVM (RBF, C = 1), CART, C4.5, RF, AdaBoost in R 2.15.0; ORC via AMPL and Gurobi 3.0.0/4.5.2; 'on par' (beats CART on 9/11, C4.5 on 5/11); lists of 11.8 rules vs 8.7 (CART) and 14.5 (C4.5) leaves; solver 'generally terminated' before optimality, gaps only for TicTacToe; Wine needed Apriori, about 20 h, RF best; untuned ORC on par with hindsight-tuned SVM (WP pp. 16-30).
positioning: Against associative classifiers that rank rules by interestingness (CBA, CMAR, CPAR), rule ensembles, LAD (confidence-one rules) and greedy trees; extends Bayardo-Agrawal's support-confidence border (WP pp. 4-5).
writing: Interpretability defined operationally with a psychology citation (Miller 1956); toy tables to explain constraints; measured 'on par' wording; decision lists rendered in words (WP pp. 2-3, 7-8, 17-22).
limits_future: MIO 'computationally intensive'; lists larger than CART's; Apriori needed at Wine scale; parameters untuned, better performance possible by varying them; claims to open optimization-based rule mining and new regularization forms (WP pp. 19, 22-26).

method_links.note: One accuracy-maximizing MIO replaces heuristic rule ordering and six incumbents are dueled with honest 'on par' wording; the hindsight-tuned SVM handicaps ORC, not the baseline; but no warm start and certification dropped ('generally terminated', gaps only for TicTacToe): Tension T1.
Conciseness has a knob (R_rank) but it is fixed at 1/L so as not to sacrifice accuracy; size and accuracy are reported separately, with no curve.
Data-mining heuristics (Apriori plus interestingness ranking) recast as MIOs over a polytope with provably integral auxiliaries; boundary printed when Apriori replaces RuleGen on Wine.
Qualitative 'why now' (computer speed advancing exponentially, cloud computing), no figure.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Mine the non-dominated support-coverage frontier, which contains the optimizer of every monotone interestingness measure, so that no measure has to be chosen.
An SVM tuned in hindsight on test accuracy is compared with the untuned ORC, which is still on par (compare S153's instances built in favour of the robust model).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: promote the evaluation metric to the training objective
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The ranking MIO maximizes (regularized) training accuracy directly instead of ordering rules by an interestingness proxy.

transferable: Show that auxiliary indicator variables are forced integral by the constraints and declare them continuous, keeping the binary count at 2d (WP p. 7).
Use no-good cuts to enumerate every optimum at a frontier point before moving the bound (WP pp. 10-11).
Add a hindsight-tuned version of the strongest baseline in an appendix; if the untuned method still competes, the comparison is robust to tuning (WP p. 27).
coauthors: Allison Chang, Cynthia Rudin (MIT ORC address)

quotes.text: trying to explain a support vector kernel to a medical doctor is not likely to persuade him to use an SVM-based diagnostic system
We generally terminated the solver before (15) solved to provable optimality.

title: Network Analysis for Predicting Academic Impact
contribution: Research-in-progress showing that citation-network centrality at publication (high betweenness, low clustering) predicts top-cited management/IS/OR papers (AUC 0.70-0.78), and that adding early-career co-authorship and citation centralities to citation counts raises the AUC for predicting career awards from 0.80 to 0.85.
problem_entry: {DA (prediction for decisions); AP (academic personnel and funding); no optimization model} Tenure and early-grant committees decide on little evidence by subjective assessment; analogies to Sabermetrics and data-driven firms; existing scholar rankings rest on citation counts (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Yearly snapshots of citation and co-authorship networks (1975-2012) give four centralities at publication or early in a career, used as logistic-regression features for top-cited papers and career awards (pp. 4-8).
assumptions: Web of Knowledge: over 700,000 papers and 2,200,000 citations in management, IS and OR journals 1975-2012 (p. 3); 250 award recipients vs over 130,000 non-recipients after removing ambiguous names (p. 8); impact = 2012 citation percentile within publication year (p. 6); random 70/30 splits (pp. 6, 8).
proof_devices: n/a (empirical): logistic regressions (eqs. 1-6, garbled in extraction) compared by ROC and AUC (pp. 6-8)
within-cohort outcome normalization (citation percentile within publication year) (p. 6)
yearly network snapshots so that features use only information available at prediction time (pp. 4-5)
experiments: Top-1% papers: betweenness ratio 7.88 at publication to 21.95 at year five, clustering ratio 0.86 to 0.44 (Table 1, p. 5); time-zero betweenness significant at 0.001 for top 0.1/0.5/1%, PageRank and closeness not; AUC 78/74/70% (pp. 6-7); awards AUC 0.80 (citations) vs 0.85 (with centralities) (p. 9); baseline total citations only; no calibration or precision reported.
positioning: Against citation-count scholar metrics (h-index, g-index, m-quotient) and early citation prediction (KDD Cup 2003, Livne et al.); borrows the data-driven-decision argument from sports analytics and Brynjolfsson et al. (2011) (pp. 2-3).
writing: Research-in-progress: rhetorical questions in abstract and introduction, 'Big Data' framing, results called 'quite surprising', first-of-its-kind claim; table numbers and model count misstated in the text (pp. 1-9).
limits_future: Future variables (content, affiliations, author order, journal rank, search and social-media signals) and an 'academic dashboard' (p. 9); unstated (my reading): random rather than temporal splits, censoring of recent careers among non-recipients, text/table numbering slips (pp. 5-8).

method_links.note: Steps 1-2 present (owners: personnel and funding committees; current rule: subjective assessment; naive quantitative baseline: citation counts), but only predictions are scored (AUC): no decision model, decision metric or field test, so mark 4 is not met.

transferable: Normalize the outcome within cohorts (citation percentile within publication year) so one model can pool papers of different ages (p. 6).
Build yearly snapshots of a growing network so that every feature uses only information available at the prediction date (pp. 4-5).
coauthors: Erik Brynjolfsson (MIT Sloan), Shachar Reichman (MIT Sloan), John M. Silberholz (MIT ORC)

quotes.text: Current academic decisions (hiring, tenure, prizes) are mostly very subjective.
We find that adding the centrality measures increases the AUC by 5 percent (0.8 for the citations count only and 0.85 for the citations + co-authorship + citation network centrality).

title: Robust and adaptive network flows
contribution: Robust and adaptive maximum-flow and minimum-cut models for networks whose arcs or nodes fail: the robust max flow is an LP, while the robust min cut, adaptive and over-time versions are NP-hard; an adaptive flow-cut game has an equilibrium, an LP gives provable approximations for path-based and adaptive flows, and on NETGEN instances it reaches about 95% of an interdiction upper bound.
problem_entry: {RO; LO (network flows); IO (cuts, interdiction); AP (pipelines, logistics) as motivation} Unlike demand or parameter uncertainty, the network structure itself fails; crude-oil pipelines 'managed manually' must deliver after the worst attack; normal operation must be a full flow, avoiding an arbitrary cost ratio when disruption probabilities are unknown (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Robust max flow with weak conservation and per-node failure budgets becomes an LP by dualizing the inner worst-case sum (Theorem 1); adaptive max flow reroutes within initial arc flows after at most Gamma failures; path-based robust flows and adaptive flows over time; Gamma here limits failing rows, so the 2003-2004 budget results do not transfer (pp. 5-9, 16-21).
assumptions: Single commodity s-t, deterministic capacities, binary arc failures with local (Sec. 2) then global budget; node failures reduced to arc failures; super-source arcs infallible (pp. 5, 8, 23); 10 NETGEN instances (sizes partly garbled in extraction) and random tree-like networks (pp. 23-24).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: LP with 2m + n - 1 variables and constraints via duality of the inner budget problem (pp. 5-6)
robust min cut strongly NP-hard via equivalence with nodewise interdiction and reduction from matching interdiction (Lemmas 1-3, Theorem 2, pp. 7-8)

adaptive value = network interdiction on flow capacities; NP-hardness and approximation hardness carry over (Lemma 5, Corollary 1, pp. 12-13); polynomial for constant Gamma and on s-t-planar graphs (pp. 11, 13); Sigma2p placement to explain a strong dual for an NP-hard problem (p. 13)
concave QP with binary extreme points, then KKT linearization with binaries or SOS for MIO solvers (Lemma 6, pp. 13-14)
adaptive min cut and a flow-vs-cut zero-sum game with equilibrium by Wald's minimax theorem (Theorems 3-4, pp. 15-16)

title: On the approximability of adjustable robust convex optimization under uncertainty
contribution: Proves that an optimal static robust solution, computable in polynomial time, is within a factor 1 + rho/s (2 for symmetric sets) of the fully adjustable optimum for two-stage and path-multistage convex problems with uncertain constraints, and within (1 + rho/s)^2 with uncertain objectives, where s and rho are the symmetry and translation factor of the uncertainty set.
problem_entry: {RO; CP (convex, SOCP/SDP instances); AP (revenue management) as motivation} Stochastic and adjustable robust problems are intractable (two-stage set covering hard to approximate within Omega(log n)); the line's earlier bounds covered only covering constraints with RHS uncertainty, missing 'packing constraints and uncertainty in constraint coefficients' as in revenue management (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Scale the adjustable optimum's first stage and its recourse at the symmetry point by alpha = 1/(1 + rho/s); the scaled solution is static-feasible for every u and concavity loses at most alpha, so the approximation factor is a geometric constant of the uncertainty set (pp. 9-13).
assumptions: (A1)-(A2) concave objectives with f(0) = 0; (A3) constraints convex in decisions, concave and increasing in u in a compact convex U in the nonnegative orthant, g(0, 0, u) = 0, max over u solvable; (A4) convex X, Y containing 0; concavity in u adopted for tractability of the static problem; covering constraints not modelled; (A5) for objective uncertainty (pp. 4-6, 15); theory only.
proof_devices: Lemmas 2-3: homogeneity inequalities f(alpha x) >= alpha f(x) and g(beta u) <= beta g(u) from concavity/convexity with zero at the origin (pp. 11-12)
Lemma 1 (from S165): every u <= (1 + rho/s) u0 for the symmetry point u0 (p. 11)
Theorem 1: z_AR <= (1 + rho/s) z_Rob (pp. 11-13)
Theorems 2 and 4: static robust problem polynomial via equivalence of separation and optimization (pp. 13, 16)
Theorem 3: (1 + rho/s)^2 under objective uncertainty (pp. 16-18)
Theorem 5: same bound for multistage problems with a path uncertainty network, proof sketched (pp. 18-20)
large-gap instance: static arbitrarily worse for the stochastic objective (p. 14)
positioning: Extends own line (S134, 2010; S165, 2011) beyond RHS-covering LPs; credits Ben-Tal et al. for adjustable policies, Feige et al. for hardness, Minkowski for symmetry; contrasts stochastic intractability (Shapiro-Nemirovski, Dyer-Stougie) (pp. 2-4, 9).
writing: Generality first: an applications gallery before the contributions; the 'first ... in such generality' claim made twice; short proofs, multistage sketched 'in the interest of space'; cross-reference slips ((4.1) for (1.2), p. 12; (4.4) for (1.3), p. 13).
limits_future: No stochastic analogue (p. 14); covering constraints excluded (p. 6); multistage only for path networks, general case asserted to extend in a straightforward manner (p. 18); no tightness example for the robust bound (my reading); the bound offered as guidance for choosing uncertainty sets (p. 20).

method_links.note: Static counterpart stays polynomially solvable, with the assumption that buys it named (concavity in u); boundary printed: covering constraints, stochastic gap, multistage beyond paths.

Solution-independent bound on the price of not adapting, indexed by set geometry and handed to the modeller for choosing the set (step 6), but no computed curve and no bad case for the robust bound; the stochastic gap example plays that role only for the stochastic objective.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: build the tractable policy from the fully adaptive optimum
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The feasible static solution is a scaled copy of the adjustable optimum (first stage plus recourse at the symmetry point), as in S165 (card s08).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: geometry of the uncertainty set explains the value of adaptivity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Symmetry and translation factor alone set the static-vs-adjustable bound; the conclusion turns this into guidance for choosing sets (compare S049, p. 4).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: power-and-limits theorem for a tractable policy class
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A power bound for static robust solutions in the robust setting paired with an unbounded-gap instance in the stochastic setting (as in S165).

transferable: To bound a static policy against the fully adaptive optimum, scale the adaptive solution toward the origin by a factor fixed by the set's geometry and use f(alpha x) >= alpha f(x) for concave f with f(0) = 0 (pp. 11-13).
Prove tractability of the robust counterpart through a separation oracle (maximize a concave function over a convex set) rather than an explicit reformulation (pp. 13, 16).
Open with a gallery of applications satisfying the assumptions (LP, revenue management, network design, QCQP, SDP) to make the generality concrete (pp. 5-9).

quotes.text: Therefore, the static solution can be arbitrarily worse as compared to a fully-adjustable solution for the stochastic optimization problem under constraint coefficient uncertainty.

Since our results relate the performance bounds to the geometric properties of the uncertainty set, they provide useful guidance towards choosing a specific uncertainty set for a particular application such that the performance of static-robust is good.
